disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive anxiety and worry about a variety of everyday events or activities, lasting for at least six months and often much longer. Individuals typically find it difficult to control the worry, which is accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations such as restlessness, fatigue, concentration problems, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. The course is often chronic and fluctuating, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to life stressors but a baseline tendency toward pervasive apprehension. GAD is distinguished from normal worry by its intensity, duration, and interference with functioning, and from other anxiety disorders by its broad, non–situation-specific focus rather than being tied to discrete fears or episodes.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Sean began seriously planning a gradual retirement from his dental practice while simultaneously investing in new digital equipment and mentoring two younger associates to take over. What he expected to be a satisfying transition instead became a prolonged period of uncertainty: patient volume fluctuated after a nearby corporate dental chain opened, his associates hesitated to commit financially to a full buy‑in, and he felt personally responsible for keeping the practice stable for his long‑term staff. Over the next 15 months, he found himself staying late to recheck treatment plans and financial projections, cutting back on hikes and painting sessions as he worried about whether he was leaving his patients and employees in a secure position. The strain became clinically significant when his preoccupation with the practice’s future began to erode his enjoyment of work, his concentration in the operatory, and his ability to relax at home, prompting his wife and a junior colleague to urge him to see a psychiatrist after he admitted he "couldn’t turn his mind off" about the office even on vacation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind is constantly racing about the practice and the future, and I just can’t shut the worrying off anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly fifteen months ago, Denise was promoted into a higher‑visibility role where she juggled multiple client accounts, tight deadlines, and frequent late‑night calls with overseas teams. At first she leaned into her usual strategy of meticulous planning and calendar‑blocking, but as project scopes kept shifting and expectations from senior partners escalated, she began extending her workday further into the night and saying yes to every request out of fear of falling behind. Over the following year, her work began to bleed into every corner of her life: she checked emails obsessively on weekends, skipped runs with her running club, and struggled to enjoy trips or evenings out because she was mentally rehearsing worst‑case scenarios about upcoming deliverables and job security. When she realized she was re‑reading the same financial models over and over without being able to focus, and a supervisor gently questioned whether she was "stretched too thin" after a small but uncharacteristic error in a client presentation, she became alarmed enough about how much her constant tension was affecting her performance to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to focus on my analyses at work—my mind keeps going blank even when I’m staring right at the spreadsheets.”

narrative.stressor: About a year and three months ago, Gregory’s store cut employee hours after a change in corporate management, and his schedule became irregular, with fluctuating shifts and reduced pay just as his wife’s hours at her job were also trimmed. The couple fell a month behind on a utility bill, and Gregory started picking up every extra shift offered, worrying constantly about keeping up with rent, car payments, and helping out his aging mother when unexpected expenses came up. Over the next year, the combination of unpredictable income, longer commutes for occasional side gigs, and his sense of responsibility to support both his household and church community slowly eroded the sense of ease he used to find in gardening, fishing, and volunteering. When he caught himself sitting at the register feeling utterly drained before his shift even started, dreading how he would make it through the day and still have energy for his family, his pastor encouraged him to talk to a doctor, and he was referred for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel worn out all the time no matter how much I rest, like I don’t have any energy left to get through work or take care of things at home.”
